query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The low hardness and strength in equimolar (or near-equimolar) CoCrFeNiTi, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability, are governed by its coarse-grained, single‐phase solid solution state. This structure permits relatively unhindered dislocation glide because the lattice distortion effect is moderate and grain boundary strengthening mechanisms (from nanocrystallinity or secondary precipitates) are absent. In contrast, HEAs that exhibit high hardness and compressive strength obtain these properties from additional strengthening via either nanocrystalline grain sizes or the formation of hard secondary phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a coarse-grained, single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply processing methods (e.g., severe plastic deformation or controlled thermal processing) to achieve significant grain refinement or introduce minor, well-dispersed precipitate phases.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature and up to 600 °C under quasi-static compressive or hardness testing loads.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size and/or the presence of nano-scale precipitates mediate the transition from dislocation-dominated deformation to grain-boundary or precipitate-hardening mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: In the coarse-grained, single-phase state, dislocation motion is relatively unimpeded because the density of barriers (grain boundaries or precipitates) is low and the lattice distortion effect is modest. Enhancing the barrier density (via finer grains or precipitates) would impede dislocation glide, thereby increasing hardness and strength while potentially reducing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Grain-refined (or precipitate-enhanced) CoCrFeNiTi samples will exhibit higher hardness and compressive strength relative to the starting coarse-grained state, with a likely trade-off of reduced ductility. The improvement should correlate inversely with grain size (or directly with precipitate volume fraction) within the tested temperature and loading conditions.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNiTi in its as-cast or conventionally processed coarse-grained, single-phase condition at room temperature, showing modest hardness and strength accompanied by high plasticity and machinability.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to equimolar/near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloys in a single-phase, solid-solution state under quasi-static mechanical loading at room temperature to 600 °C; it may not hold for alloys already containing multiphase structures or under very dynamic loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of grain-size reduction or precipitate addition on the balance of strength and ductility is uncertain due to processing variability. Additionally, the optimum levels for grain refinement or precipitate formation to maximize strength without excessively compromising ductility remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiTi samples: one set in the standard processed coarse-grained state and another set processed to attain a nanocrystalline (or finely precipitated) microstructure. Conduct identical nanoindentation, compressive, and ductility tests at room temperature and up to 600 °C.
measurements: Grain size and phase distribution by electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction
Compressive strength through standardized mechanical tests
Ductility from strain-to-failure measurements in compression
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the grain-refined or precipitate-containing samples do not show a significant increase in hardness and compressive strength (or if ductility does not decrease correspondingly) compared to the coarse-grained baseline, then the hypothesis—that the low strength originates from the coarse-grained, dislocation-glide-dominated structure—would be falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Findings: The addition of 4.2 at% Cr led to the formation of a Laves phase in addition to the BCC phase, whereas the base alloy was single-phase BCC.; The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 reached 535.8 Hv0.3, which is 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr (460.1 Hv0.3).; The yield strength of HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 reached 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa, which is 207.5 MPa higher than HfMoTaTi

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
